stem: In science, a model is best described as
options: a simplified view of a system that keeps what matters
an exact copy of a system with every detail kept
a final description of nature that never changes
a small toy built only for display in a classroom
explanation: Correct option: (A). Models are simplified ways of looking at real systems that focus only on what is most important for a given question. They are not exact copies, they can be improved as more detail is added, and they need not be physical toys.

stem: When studying the basic effect of gravity on a falling object, which factor is commonly neglected in a simple model?

The height from which it falls
Air resistance on the object

stem: You want to model whether a ball hit by a batter will cross the boundary without touching the ground. Which set of details matters most?
options: Brand of the bat, colour of the ball and grass length
Mass of the ball, and its speed and direction of hit
Stitching on the seam, colour of the ball and its spin
Name of the bowler, the pitch and the time of the day
explanation: Correct option: (B). Whether the ball carries the boundary depends mainly on its mass and the speed and direction in which it is hit. Bat brand, ball colour and grass make no difference, while spin and seam stitching have small effects that a simple model can ignore.

stem: To understand how the heart pumps blood, a biologist ignores the working of the individual cells in it. This choice is
options: a mistake, because cells are the basic units of life
a deliberate simplification to study the heart as one system
unscientific, because a model must include every cell
acceptable only if the cells are too small to be seen
explanation: Correct option: (B). Ignoring individual cells lets the organ be understood as a functioning system; such choices are made on purpose, not by mistake. A model never has to include every detail, and the reason for ignoring cells is the question being asked, not their size.

stem: An aircraft needing 22,300 kg of fuel ran short because the ground crew used fuel density in pounds per litre instead of kilograms per litre. What does this incident show most clearly?
options: Fuel density changes a lot during a flight
Using one standard unit system avoids costly errors
Pounds and kilograms are equal for liquid fuels

explanation: Correct option: (B). The mix-up of pounds and kilograms left the plane about 15,000 litres short. Using standard SI units everywhere avoids such conversions and errors. Pounds and kilograms are very different, and the problem was the unit, not the use of mass or a change in density.

stem: Varsha says, "It will rain this afternoon because the clouds look dark." Which question would make her prediction most scientifically testable?
options: Do you really feel sure that it will rain?
Will it rain today, yes or no?
Was humidity above 80 per cent last time it rained?
Do the clouds look darker than they did yesterday?
explanation: Correct option: (C). Good scientific questions ask for measurable data and past patterns, such as humidity when it last rained. Asking about feelings or a yes/no outcome adds no evidence, and 'looking darker' is still an unmeasured impression.

stem: A message claims that food becomes harmful if eaten during an eclipse. Which approach best tests this claim scientifically?
options: Ask whether the eclipse causes any physical change in food
Count how many people have forwarded the message
Accept it because the claim has been around for years
Reject it because the person sending it seems unfriendly
explanation: Correct option: (A). An eclipse is just a play of shadows, so the scientific test asks what physical, chemical or biological change it could cause in food; none supports the claim. Popularity, age of a claim or the sender's manner are not evidence.

stem: What is the main purpose of making a rough estimate in science?
options: To replace every exact measurement
To check if an answer makes sense
To avoid using numbers altogether
To get the exact value very quickly
explanation: Correct option: (B). An approximate estimate tells us whether a result is reasonable or impossible and helps detect errors. It does not replace exact measurements where they are needed, it still uses numbers, and it is by nature not exact.

stem: About how many minutes are there in one day?
explanation: Correct option: (C). One day has 24 hours and each hour has 60 minutes, so 60 x 24 = 1440 minutes. 360 and 3600 confuse minutes with other counts (3600 is the number of seconds in an hour), and 8640 is the litres in the balloon estimate.

stem: A person at rest takes about 14 breaths per minute, and each breath is about 0.5 litre. Roughly how much air is breathed in one day?
options: About 1,000 litres
About 100 litres
About 100,000 litres
About 10,000 litres
explanation: Correct option: (D). Breaths per day = 14 x 1440, about 20,000. Air per day = 20,000 x 0.5 litre = 10,000 litres. 100 and 1,000 litres are too small by factors of 100 and 10, and 100,000 litres is ten times too large.

stem: A student estimates that a family of four needs about 100 g of rice for a whole month. What is the best judgement of this estimate?
options: It is far too little to be reasonable
It is reasonable for a rough estimate
It is far too much to be reasonable
It cannot be judged without exact data
explanation: Correct option: (A). Each adult needs about 2000-2500 kcal a day, and 100 g of rice supplies only a small part of one person's daily need, so 100 g for four people for a month is clearly far too little. Estimation lets us judge this without exact data.

stem: One balloon holds about 2 litres and can be filled about 3 times a minute. A second estimate of daily breathing using this gives about 8640 litres, while the first gave about 10,000 litres. What should be concluded?
options: The first estimate is wrong because the two differ
Both are wrong because neither is an exact value
The two estimates agree reasonably well
The second must be right because it uses balloons
explanation: Correct option: (C). 3 balloons/min x 2 litres x 1440 min = 8640 litres, which is close to 10,000 litres for estimation purposes, so the two checks agree reasonably. Estimates are not expected to match exactly, so a small difference does not make either one wrong.
